facts.claim: One RTX 4090 tried 21,975.5 million SHA-256 guesses a second in Chick3nman’s hashcat 6.2.6 benchmark (October 2022).
The same RTX 4090 benchmark (October 2022) tried 8,865.7 thousand PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 guesses a second at 999 iterations.
OWASP’s Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, with a unique random salt for every password.
OWASP: with salts, nobody can tell whether two users share a password without cracking the hashes, and precomputed tables stop working.
NIST SP 800-132 (December 2010) recommended a PBKDF2 iteration count of at least 1,000.
RFC 8018 (2017) specifies PBKDF2: the iteration count makes every password guess cost that many rounds.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 (August 2025): a site SHALL check a new password against a blocklist of commonly used, expected or compromised passwords.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 (August 2025): a site allows no more than 100 failed sign-in attempts in a row on one account.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 (August 2025): one-time codes are not phishing-resistant; WebAuthn keys, as in passkeys, are bound to the real site’s name.
RFC 6238 (2011): a time-based one-time password is an HMAC of a shared secret and the current 30-second step.
RFC 6265 (2011): an HttpOnly cookie is hidden from page scripts, and a Secure cookie is sent only over encrypted connections.
RFC 6749 (2012), OAuth 2.0: the authorization code flow sends the browser away to sign in and back with a short-lived code.
RFC 7636 (2015), PKCE: the code challenge is the SHA-256 of a secret verifier, so a stolen code is useless without it.
RFC 9700 (January 2025), OAuth security best practice: public clients MUST use PKCE, and every client MUST prevent cross-site request forgery.
OpenID Connect Core 1.0: the site must check the ID token’s signature, and that its audience names the site’s own client id.
